common_name: Gold Standard Hosta (Classic Gold-Centered Green-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gold Standard is one of the most widely planted variegated hosta cultivars, with leaves that emerge chartreuse-green and mature to a bright golden-yellow center edged in a contrasting dark green margin.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the brightest gold color. Gold Standard is one of the most enduringly popular variegated hosta cultivars, producing medium-to-large clumps of heart-shaped leaves that emerge chartreuse-green in spring and brighten through the season to a vivid golden-yellow center framed by a distinct, contrasting dark green margin, a striking color transformation that provides changing seasonal interest from a single planting. Pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage on tall scapes in mid-to-late summer. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic coloring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage, and apply iron phosphate bait around vulnerable new growth if damage appears.
sources: American Hosta Society — Gold Standard Cultivar Notes

common_name: Stained Glass Hosta (Fragrant Gold-Centered Hosta of the Year)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stained Glass was named Hosta of the Year in 2006 for its large, glossy, gold-centered leaves with a wavy blue-green margin and its unusually fragrant white flowers, a rare trait among hostas.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best gold color. Stained Glass was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 2006, recognized for large, glossy, rounded leaves with a bright golden-yellow center bordered by a wavy, blue-green margin, along with fragrant, near-white flowers on tall scapes in summer — a genuinely useful trait, since most hostas have little to no fragrance. Its large, well-proportioned clump size and reliable, vigorous growth make it an excellent specimen or anchor plant in a shade border. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic coloring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage, and apply iron phosphate bait around vulnerable new growth if damage appears.

common_name: Great Expectations Hosta (Large Gold-Centered Blue-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Great Expectations was named Hosta of the Year in 1998 for its large, thick, corrugated leaves with a creamy gold center and irregular blue-green margin, one of the most dramatic large hosta cultivars available.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best center color. Great Expectations was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 1998, celebrated for its large, thick, heavily corrugated leaves with a broad, creamy-gold to chartreuse center bordered by an irregular, wavy blue-green margin, creating a bold, three-dimensional textural and color display in the shade garden. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. As a sport of the popular blue hosta Sum and Substance, it inherits vigorous, substantial growth, forming a large, imposing clump over time that works well as a specimen or focal point. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sagae was named Hosta of the Year in 2000 for its large, upright, vase-shaped clump of blue-green leaves broadly margined in creamy white to gold, one of the most architecturally striking hosta cultivars available.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best margin color. Sagae was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 2000, prized for its distinctive upright, vase-shaped growth habit — unusual among hostas, most of which form low, spreading mounds — with large, glossy, blue-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that often deepens to soft gold as the season progresses. Tall scapes of pale lavender flowers rise well above the foliage in summer. Its architectural, upright form and large mature size make it an excellent specimen or focal point at the back of a shade border, distinct in silhouette from the many mound-forming hosta cultivars. The margin coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

common_name: Praying Hands Hosta (Narrow Upright Twisted-Leaf Novelty Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Praying Hands is a distinctive novelty hosta with narrow, upright, twisted leaves that stay folded together along the midrib, resembling hands held in prayer, a striking departure from typical flat hosta foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade. Praying Hands is one of the most distinctive novelty hostas available, its narrow, dark green, gold-margined leaves staying folded together along the center vein rather than opening flat, so each leaf remains upright and twisted in a shape that closely resembles two hands pressed together in prayer. This unusual leaf form gives the plant a strong vertical, sculptural presence quite unlike the typical broad, spreading hosta mound, making it a conversation-piece accent in a shade border or container planting. Lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its narrow, upright habit takes up relatively little horizontal space compared to standard hostas, making it useful for tight spots where a bolder, spreading hosta would not fit. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.
